STAMP (2018) explicitly combines the latest item embedding with broader session context: the session-wide mean and latest embedding condition attention over item embeddings; transformed attentive context and latest-item vectors interact multiplicatively before candidate scoring. Thus, its mean pooling covers the entire session, not a recent window, and its context lacks explicit ordering beyond identifying the last item. This is a close precedent for an explicit recent-item readout, rather than evidence that recent-window averaging improves it. [Author implementation](https://github.com/uestcnlp/STAMP/blob/master/model/STAMP_rsc.py).

NARM (2017) retains an order-sensitive GRU: its final hidden state represents global sequential behavior and conditions attention over preceding GRU states. The final state and attentive sum are concatenated for bilinear candidate scoring. “Local” therefore means selectively attended context, not a fixed recent window or raw latest-item embedding. Table 4 compares global-only, local-only and hybrid representations; hybrid wins across all three dataset settings at both tested dimensions. On Diginetica, d=100, Recall@20 is 61.88, 61.71 and 62.58, respectively. These are component ablations, not parameter-matched comparisons. [NARM paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.04725).

I did not establish a published four-way, parameter-matched comparison in these sources. For the GRU4Rec experiment, the discriminating controls would hold the backbone and training fixed and compare: latest-item residual; masked recent-k embedding mean with k=1 included; order-sensitive encoding of the same window; and latest-item versus window readouts using identical gates/projections and matched parameter budgets. Include full-history mean and a shuffled-window control, preserving the latest item. These proposed controls separate additional history, recency, ordering and readout capacity; each variant remains one jointly trained network.
